description: We are interested to map the fires on the earth.
summary:
Fires are growing. Europe had its worst fire year on record in 2025, the USA has burned nearly twice as much this year as last, and in July 2026 over 300,000 people fled fires in France and Spain. A firefighter, who has worked for 20 years in the sector, told us crews check about ten websites, and their top need is prevention: knowing where fire will start tomorrow.

NASA’s fire record is split: VIIRS, flying since 2012, sees 2.7 times more fire than MODIS, flying since 2000. Emerge harmonizes the two into one fair calendar from 2000 to today, for any place on Earth, with an error range on every estimate.

Emerge brings more than 20 data sources, half of them from NASA, into one app: 25 years of fire history, fires burning now, tomorrow’s risk, rain, wind, temperature, humidity, soil moisture, plant greenness, land type and official fire reports.

We tackle one of firefighters’ top problems: knowing where fire will start tomorrow. We built and trained our own machine learning model that weighs 20 variables for every spot on Earth, covering fire weather, 25 years of fire history, recent fires nearby, land type and season. Tested on 2025, a year it never saw, it caught nearly twice as many new fires as NASA’s fire-weather index.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Emerge is a web app that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one burning activity calendar for any place on Earth, so the satellite that made a detection no longer matters and trends, anomalies and seasonal patterns become the focus. The record runs from November 2000 to 14 November 2026, and the live map adds NASA’s latest fire detections within hours. It also gives an next-day fire-risk prediction, tested against real fires.

The challenge problem: NASA’s fire record is split between two instruments. MODIS has watched fires since 2000 at about 1 km. VIIRS has flown since 2012 at 375 m, sees smaller fires, and records about 2.7 times more fire. Joined naively, fire seems to triple after 2012 when only the instrument changed. And as MODIS retires, its 11 MODIS-only years (2000–2012) risk becoming unusable.

How we harmonize it:

  1. We processed 461 million NASA FIRMS detections, keeping vegetation fires only.
  2. Using the years both instruments flew, we learned how MODIS relates to VIIRS for each country, latitude band and month.
  3. We converted the MODIS-only years to VIIRS level, with an error range on every estimate.
  4. We tested this on years it had never seen.

What users get: they pick a country, click a point, type latitude and longitude, or draw an area, then choose a date range. They see:

  • a calendar of years × months, with colour steps labelled by number and a table view of the same numbers, so the busiest months and years stand out;
  • hotspots, fire days, or each satellite separately, with measured and estimated years marked;
  • “Is this unusual?”: this month against the median and average of past years, naming the years compared;
  • the current fire against the same days in every past year, and a season-so-far chart;
  • fires detected next to fires officially reported;
  • downloads: hotspots, monthly numbers and a summary as CSV, plus the calendar and charts as images.

Tomorrow’s risk: we built and trained our own machine learning model that weighs 20 variables for every land square with vegetation, about 28 km across: fire weather, 25 years of fire history, recent fires nearby, land type and season. It ranks the highest-risk spots in every region of the world, each with a plain reason. Places already burning show the fire and a downwind arrow.

What benefits does it have?

  • One place instead of ten websites: more than 20 data sources, half of them from NASA. They cover fire history, fires now, tomorrow’s risk, a week outlook, rain, wind, temperature, humidity, soil moisture, plant greenness and land type.
  • Better forecasts: tested on 2025, a year the model never saw, it caught 20.4% of new fires in its top spots. NASA’s fire-weather index, which uses weather alone, caught 11.2%, so ours caught nearly twice as many. Fire history caught 16.7% and random picks 10.5%; in Europe, 53.8% against 41.1% for the index.
  • A record you can trust: on unseen years, monthly errors were about 20% in Bulgaria and 14% in the USA, and our 90% ranges held about 95% of the time.
  • Open proof: a public page shows every result, including what doesn’t work yet: https://emergefire.app/proof

What is the intended impact?
Fires are growing:

  • 2025 was Europe’s worst fire year on record;
  • the USA has burned nearly twice as much this year as last;
  • in July 2026 over 300,000 people fled fires in France and Spain.

A firefighter with 20 years of experience told us crews check about ten websites, and their top need is prevention: knowing where fire will start tomorrow, so teams can be there first. Emerge serves early warning and emergency responders, fire services, land managers and scientists: to plan before the season, spot unusual conditions, and position crews a day ahead. The same method works in every country, and the record continues on VIIRS as MODIS retires.

What tools did we use?

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, SQL.
  • Data and model: DuckDB, pandas, scikit-learn, LightGBM (machine learning).
  • Website: Next.js, React, MapLibre and deck.gl (maps), in English and Bulgarian.
  • Hosting and code: Vercel (emergefire.app), GitHub (open source, Apache 2.0).
  • Data: NASA FIRMS, GFWED, GIBS, POWER, IMERG, SMAP; Copernicus EFFIS and GWIS; NIFC; Bulgaria’s Forest Agency; Open-Meteo.
  • Video: Remotion and ElevenLabs.
  • Hardware: none, just laptops.

How is it creative?
Today’s tools keep the satellites apart. FIRMS and Global Forest Watch show MODIS and VIIRS side by side, and GWIS works mainly by country. The only fire calendar we found covers 20 countries, uses MODIS only, and stops in 2022.

Emerge is the first we know of to:

  • join both satellites into one fair record from 2000 to today, for any point or drawn area, with an error range on every estimate;
  • predict where new fires will start tomorrow with our own machine learning model (20 variables, not weather alone);
  • check it in public against NASA’s fire-weather index, history and random picks, showing where it wins and where it loses;
  • replace ten websites with one screen: fire history, tomorrow’s risk, weather, fires now and wind direction for any point.

The idea came from a firefighter: we built what he said he was missing.

What did we consider?

  • Real users: the forecast is built around a firefighter’s needs.
  • Fair testing: only on unseen years, always against simple alternatives.
  • Honesty: estimates and weak spots are marked. It’s a research prototype, not an official warning.
  • Clear data: “no data” is never shown as “zero fires”, and satellite numbers and official reports are labelled apart.
  • Easy access: free, no login, works on phones, English and Bulgarian.
  • Open source: Apache 2.0 licence, every source credited.
